papers.title_in_file: Quantum Semi-Random Forests for Qubit-Efficient Recommender Systems
papers.version_note: arXiv:2508.00027v1 [quant-ph], 30 Jul 2025. The text layer is damaged in places: equations 1 to 3 lost their summation signs, Algorithm 1 is flattened, the sentence about sparsity on the ICM matrix is garbled (the percent sign and a clause are lost), Key Takeaway 3 ends at 'using 90', and a flat exponent such as 10-3 stands for ten to the minus three. The paper uses the names QsRF and QsRL for the same model, and says 'three-stage' in the abstract while describing four stages (Stage 1 to Stage 4).
papers.what_it_is: A short arXiv preprint that compresses item tags with a 1000-atom learned dictionary, selects 5 atoms with a depth-3 QAOA run on the PennyLane simulator, and scores recommendations with a bagged-tree ensemble on the QuantumCLEF ICM-150 and ICM-500 benchmarks.

existing.note: The Conclusion makes the claim as stored, but the abstract says only 'performing similarly to the state-of-the-art methods', and the tables do not support 'consistently outperforms' on every metric: QsRF's AUC and Log-Loss entries on ICM-150 and ICM-500 are the weakest in Tables III and IV, and only nDCG@10 is higher. The claim rests on nDCG@10.
existing.value: The authors state in the Conclusion that on both the ICM-150 and ICM-500 splits QsRL consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art Quantum-based method; the abstract says the method performs similarly to the state-of-the-art methods.
quotes: On both the ICM-150 and ICM-500 splits of our content–metadata benchmark, QsRL consistently outperforms state of the art Quantum-based method.
while performing similarly to the stateof-the-art methods
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; the abstract and the conclusion word it differently.
existing.reader_inference: The two statements differ ('similarly' against 'consistently outperforms'). Tables III and IV list QsRF with lower AUC and higher Log-Loss than the baseline entries in the same columns, so only the nDCG@10 column favors QsRF.

existing.note: The numbers are right. The paper states they are for the ICM–500 dataset (the stored value names no dataset), and Table IV gives them as the mean of 5 seeds, with the nDCG@10 a per-user (macro) value.
existing.value: The authors report that on the ICM–500 dataset QsRF yielded AUC = 0.8260, LogLoss = 0.2372, and nDCG@10 = 0.5942.

we train an ensemble of T = 200 decision trees under bagging [16].

assertions.value: The authors state that they present a three-stage hybrid machine learning algorithm that compresses tag profiles, optimizes feature selection under a fixed qubit budget via QAOA, and scores recommendations with a Quantum semi-Random Forest built on just five qubits.
quotes: We close this gap with a three-stage hybrid machine learning algorithm that compresses tag profiles, optimizes feature selection under a fixed qubit budget via QAOA
scores recommendations with a Quantum semi-Random Forest (QsRF) built on just five qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of what the method is and its scope (Abstract).
assertions.reader_inference: The body describes four stages (Stage 1 to Stage 4), not three.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QAOA step requires exactly five qubits and that their dense 20×20 QUBO matrix fits comfortably on five logical qubits.
assertions.anchor: Section I-B, p.2; Section II-C(a), p.3
quotes: then conduct feature selection with a depth-3 QAOA that requires exactly five qubits
yields a dense 20×20 QUBO matrix Q = − diag(w) + µ 11⊤ that fits comfortably on five logical qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' claim; the paper gives no circuit encoding that maps 20 binary variables onto five qubits.
assertions.reader_inference: The mask z has one binary variable per candidate atom (20 of them) and the cost Hamiltonian is a sum of Z_i Z_j terms over the same indices as Q, which is the standard one-qubit-per-variable encoding and needs 20 qubits. The paper shows no encoding that reduces this to five. The headline 'five qubits' figure is therefore unsupported as written; this bears directly on the title claim.

assertions.value: The authors define a binary mask over the candidate set of Ktop = 20 atoms with a budget of k = 5, an energy with a penalty weight of about ten cubed that enforces selecting exactly k atoms, and a dense 20×20 matrix Q equal to − diag(w) + µ 11⊤.
assertions.anchor: Section II-B and II-C(a), Eq. (3), p.3
quotes: The Ktop = 20 highest-scoring atoms constitute the candidate set T that will be fed to the quantum search.
Let z ∈ {0, 1}Ktop be a binary mask over T and k = 5 the desired budget.
yields a dense 20×20 QUBO matrix Q = − diag(w) + µ 11⊤
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the QUBO in Section II-C(a).
assertions.reader_inference: As written, Eq. (3) is a linear term plus a penalty that depends only on the number of selected atoms, so its minimum is the top-k atoms by weight w_j, which a sort finds classically; the QAOA step then has nothing to add. This is also the paper's own fallback rule. Algorithm 1 states a different Q (see algorithm1-qubo-differs).

assertions.value: The paper gives two different forms of the QUBO matrix: Section II-C gives Q = − diag(w) + µ 11⊤, and the algorithm box gives Q = w w⊤ + µI.
assertions.anchor: Section II-C(a), p.3; Algorithm 1, line 13, p.4
quotes: yields a dense 20×20 QUBO matrix Q = − diag(w) + µ 11⊤
form QUBO Q = w w⊤ + µI
assertions.certainty_reason: Both forms are the paper's own definitions, quoted from the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say which form was run. The two give different optimisation problems.

assertions.value: The authors define the performance-driven weight of atom j as the drop in per-user nDCG@10 when that atom is removed, averaged over a bootstrap of 20% of the training rows, and take the highest-scoring atoms as the candidate set for the quantum search.
quotes: For each atom j, let δu(j) = nDCG@10(u) − nDCG@10(−j)(u) denote the drop in ranking quality for user
of 20% of the training rows yields the performance-driven
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition the paper's results depend on (Section II-B).

assertions.value: The authors state they use depth-p = 3 QAOA with parameters optimised on the validation split by SPSA using 128 shots per objective evaluation; the algorithm box states 200 shots.
assertions.anchor: Section II-C(b), p.3; Algorithm 1, line 14, p.4
quotes: We employ the depth-p = 3 Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm [14].
using 128 shots per objective evaluation
run depth-3 QAOA (200 shots) → 5-bit mask
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own QAOA setup, with a shot count that differs between the text and Algorithm 1.
assertions.reader_inference: 128 shots in the text and 200 in Algorithm 1; the paper does not reconcile them.

assertions.value: The authors state that the measured bit-string is accepted if the number of selected atoms equals k, and otherwise they fall back to the top-k atoms by weight.
quotes: Measurement returns a bit-string zˆ; if j zˆj = k the corresponding atoms are accepted, otherwise we fall back to the top-k by wj.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the selection rule in Section II-C(b).
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not report how often the fallback fired, so the results do not show how much of the selection came from the quantum circuit rather than the classical ranking. The top-k atoms by weight are what Eq. (3) as written minimises.

assertions.value: The authors define the QsRF as a bagged ensemble of decision trees on the five-dimensional codes, where each tree receives a bootstrap of the training rows and a random perturbation of the feature indices, and the predicted click-through probability is the arithmetic mean over all tree outputs.
quotes: Each tree receives a bootstrap of the training rows and a random perturbation of the feature indices, mimicking the stochasticity of classical Random Forests
At inference time the predicted click-through probability for a user–item pair is the arithmetic mean over all tree outputs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the model in Section II-D.
assertions.reader_inference: The trees are classical; the quantum part is only the feature-selection step.

assertions.value: The authors give the ensemble as 100 shallow decision trees (10 runs × 10 trees) in the contribution list and T = 200 decision trees in the methodology section.
assertions.anchor: Section I-B item 3, p.2; Section II-D, p.3
quotes: ensemble of 100 shallow decision trees (10 runs × 10 trees)
we train an ensemble of T = 200 decision trees under bagging [16].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statements of its setup, which disagree.
assertions.reader_inference: The runtime list also says 100 shallow trees (depth=8). The tree count behind the reported tables is not settled.

assertions.value: The authors state that the rows of the sketch are clustered into K = 50 sets and that for each cluster a sub-dictionary of A = 20 atoms is learned, giving a 1000-atom master atom pool.
assertions.anchor: Section II-A(b),(c), p.3; Section I-B item 1, p.2
quotes: The rows of Z are clustered into K = 50 disjoint sets
we learn a sub-dictionary Dc ∈ RM×A with A = 20 atoms by solving
that builds a 1000-atom dictionary capturing > 97% of tag-profile variance
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup (Section II-A).
assertions.reader_inference: The stated shapes do not fit: Z is the rank-32 sketch of X, yet Eq. (1) subtracts Theta times D transposed, which has 150 columns, from the rows of Z. The text layer also lost the equation's sums, so the shapes cannot be checked further.

assertions.value: The authors state that the top 32 singular vectors capture more than 97 % of the training variance of the item–tag matrix, citing the randomized SVD of Halko et al.
assertions.anchor: Section I-B, p.2; Section II-A(a), p.3
quotes: the top 32 singular vectors already capture more than 97 % of the training variance [13]
while preserving > 97 % of the Frobenius energy
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement; no variance table or plot is shown in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says 'variance' in one place and 'Frobenius energy' in another; the two are not the same quantity unless the data are centered.

assertions.value: The authors state that the randomised SVD step reduces both memory and time complexity from O(N M) to O(N d2), where the text layer prints the square of d flat, with d = 32.
quotes: This step reduces both memory and time complexity from O(N M ) to O(N d2)
we first compute a rank-d sketch Z = XVd with d = 32
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without a derivation in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: With d = 32, d squared is 1024 and M is 150, so O(N d^2) is larger than O(N M), not smaller. The stated reduction does not hold for these sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the 1000-atom dictionary enables an approximately 90% reduction in qubit usage.
assertions.anchor: Section I-B item 1, p.2; Section III-G item 3, p.6
quotes: that builds a 1000-atom dictionary capturing > 97% of tag-profile variance, enabling a ≈ 90% reduction in qubit usage
3) QsRF achieves comparable or better recommendation quality using 90
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the text gives no calculation for the 90%.
assertions.reader_inference: Going from 130 or 150 qubits to 5 is about a 96% cut, not 90%. The text layer cuts Key Takeaway 3 off after '90'.

assertions.value: The authors report that ICM–150 has 1 881 users, 5 000 items, 64 890 interactions, 150 tags and 88.6 % sparsity, and that ICM–500 has 1 889 users, 7 000 items, 68 062 interactions, 500 tags and 93.4 % sparsity.

assertions.reader_inference: The cluster sizes in Table II (up to 94 633 rows) and Section III-E (up to 123 399) exceed the interactions in Table I (64 890 and 68 062), so the rows of X are not the interactions of Table I; the paper does not say how its rows are defined.

The training portion is further split 80 / 20 into a learning set and a validation set

with standard errors below ±0.002 nDCG and thus omitted for clarity.

assertions.reader_inference: No variance is shown for any result, and the two statements give different bounds. The ICM-500 per-user standard deviation is 0.260 (Table VI), which is a different quantity from a standard error over seeds.

assertions.value: The authors state that each 20-atom cluster dictionary gave reconstruction errors consistently below 3 × 10−3 (two orders of magnitude smaller than the variance of the raw TF–IDF vectors), and that this confirms the 1000-atom global dictionary effectively preserves critical information.
assertions.anchor: Section III-A, p.4; Section III-G item 1, p.6
quotes: Each cluster was encoded with a 20-atom dictionary, yielding reconstruction errors consistently below 3 × 10−3—two orders of magnitude smaller than the variance of the raw TF–IDF vectors.

assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the raw TF–IDF variance it is compared with is not reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The final model uses 5 selected atoms, not the 1000-atom dictionary, so the reconstruction error of the 1000-atom pool does not describe the codes the trees see.

assertions.value: The authors report that on ICM–150 the QAOA energies remain between 5.01 × 10−3 and 5.03 × 10−3, that all runs yielded the same nDCG@10 score (0.1483), which they say indicates a flat local optimum, and that this eliminates the need for multi-seed ensembling.
assertions.anchor: Section III-B, Fig. 3, p.4 to p.5
quotes: On ICM–150, energies remain between 5.01 × 10−3 and 5.03 × 10−3, demonstrating strong stability and convergence.
All runs yielded the same nDCG@10 score (0.1483), indicating a flat local optimum in the QUBO solution space.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Ten runs that all give the same nDCG@10 are consistent with the same atoms being chosen each time, for example by the top-k fallback or because the objective has one obvious optimum; the paper does not show which.

assertions.value: The authors report that on ICM–500 ten depth-3 QAOA runs produced energies from 9.4 × 10−3 to 0.43, while the Figure 3 caption says the spread goes up to 0.20.

while ICM–500 shows a wider spread up to 0.20.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, with a text and caption that differ.
assertions.reader_inference: The maximum energy is 0.43 in the text and 0.20 in the caption; the paper does not reconcile them.

assertions.value: The authors state that five-qubit depth-3 QAOA consistently reaches the optimal solution for their performance-based QUBO.

assertions.reader_inference: The text reports no brute-force or classical comparison of the selected subsets, so optimality is not shown. See the notes on the qubit count and on Eq. (3).

Either way, QsRF's AUC (0.8413) is below both baseline entries and its Log-Loss (0.2300) is above both, so Table III does not support the contribution-list claim of 'superior nDCG@10, AUC, and Log-Loss'.

assertions.value: The authors state that QsRF consistently outperforms the five-feature Random Forest baseline on both datasets in AUC and Log-Loss while achieving comparable or superior nDCG@10, and in the Conclusion give ROC-AUC (∆ ≃ +0.02), LogLoss (∆ ≃ −0.02) and ICM-500 macro-nDCG@10 (∆ ≃ +0.02–0.15) gains.

in ROC-AUC (∆ ≃ +0.02), LogLoss (∆ ≃ −0.02)
on ICM-500 with macro-nDCG@10 (∆ ≃ +0.02–0.15)

assertions.reader_inference: Table V contradicts parts of this: on ICM–150 the RF nDCG@10 (0.5929) is much higher than QsRL's (0.1483), so 'comparable or superior' fails there; on ICM–500 the nDCG@10 gain is 0.0025 (0.5942 against 0.5917), not 0.02 to 0.15; the AUC and Log-Loss gains on ICM–500 are about 0.006 and 0.013, not 0.02.

assertions.value: The authors report on an 8-core laptop (Apple M2, 32 GB RAM) that dictionary learning completes in about 6 min, sparse encoding in <90 s, ten SPSA runs add <60 s, tree training takes about 20 s, and the full pipeline takes 8–12 min wall-clock.

ten SPSA runs add <60 s

assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, run on a simulator.
assertions.reader_inference: These times are for a classical simulation of the circuit, so they say nothing about the cost of running on quantum hardware.

assertions.value: The authors give the end-to-end runtime three ways: 8–12 min on an 8-core laptop (Section II-E), approximately 20 minutes on a 6-core laptop with QAOA training and inference taking 15 minutes (Section III-F), and under 15 minutes on a standard 8-core laptop (Conclusion).

The entire ICM–QsRL pipeline completes in approximately 20 minutes on a 6-core laptop
QAOA training and inference: 15 minutes
the entire pipeline runs in under 15 minutes on a standard 8-core laptop
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study whose runtime statements disagree.
assertions.reader_inference: Section II-E calls QAOA negligible (<60 s) while Section III-F gives 15 minutes for QAOA training and inference; the paper does not reconcile these.

assertions.value: The authors state an order-of-magnitude (≈ 10×) reduction in end-to-end runtime versus CAQUBO and MIQUBO, comparing with the 2-hour wall time of CAQUBO reported in prior work, and in the Conclusion call the pipeline orders of magnitude faster than previously reported quantum annealer timings.

Compared to the 2-hour wall time of CAQUBO [1]
orders of magnitude faster than previously reported quantum annealer timings
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the competing runtime is taken from another paper and the paper gives no MIQUBO runtime.
assertions.reader_inference: 2 hours against 20 minutes is 6 times, against 8–12 minutes about 10 to 15 times; 'orders of magnitude' is not supported. The comparison mixes the paper's laptop simulation with a number from another paper on different hardware.

assertions.reader_inference: No section, table or figure in the text reports an ablation over dictionary rank, bootstrap size or QAOA depth. There is also no run with the QAOA step replaced by classical top-k selection, which is the comparison that would show whether the quantum step matters.

assertions.value: The authors state that for their 20×20 performance-driven QUBO, minor embedding on an annealer would raise the effective budget from 5 logical qubits to >60 physical qubits, and that gate-based devices avoid minor embedding.
quotes: For our 20×20 performance-driven QUBO this would raise the effective budget from 5 logical qubits to >60 physical qubits
Gate-based devices avoid minor embedding: the five logical qubits are mapped one-to-one onto hardware
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim, with no calculation shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives 5 logical qubits for a QUBO with 20 binary variables; see five-qubit-claim-vs-20-variable-qubo.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Pelofske et al., that annealers outperform one-round QAOA on ∼ 100-qubit Ising benchmarks, and that deeper (p ≥ 3) QAOA with noise-aware angle optimisation starts to close that gap.
quotes: Although recent studies show that annealers outperform one-round QAOA on ∼ 100-qubit Ising benchmarks [11]
deeper (p ≥ 3) QAOA with noise-aware angle optimisation starts to close that gap
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work; the second clause has no citation.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Harrigan et al., that depth-2 QAOA was executed on 23 superconducting qubits, validating theoretical predictions but exposing depth-related locality issues, and that a definitive advantage over classical solvers is still elusive.
quotes: Harrigan et al. executed depth-2 QAOA on 23 superconducting qubits, validating theoretical predictions but exposing depth-related locality issues [9].
yet a definitive advantage over classical solvers is still elusive
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Ferrari Dacrema et al., that QPU, hybrid, simulated-annealing and tabu-search solvers were compared on up to 5 000 features and quantum approaches were found merely competitive once problem sizes required decomposition.
quotes: Ferrari Dacrema et al. systematically compared QPU, hybrid, simulated-annealing and tabu-search solvers on up to 5 000 features
found quantum approaches merely competitive once problem sizes required decomposition [10]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors describe QsRL in the Conclusion as a novel quantum-inspired sparse ranking pipeline that combines classical clustering with a five-qubit QAOA backend to learn compact, user-specific dictionaries.
quotes: we have introduced QsRL, a novel quantuminspired sparse ranking pipeline that combines classical clustering with a five-qubit QAOA backend
to learn compact, user–specific dictionaries
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own description of their method.
assertions.reader_inference: The method section describes one global dictionary, not user-specific dictionaries. The paper calls the method both 'Quantum' and 'quantum-inspired'.

assertions.value: The authors state that lower-energy QAOA solutions cluster tightly and yield stable ranking quality, and that sampling 100 users at random demonstrates that the method generalizes across diverse profile sparsities.
quotes: lower-energy QAOA solutions cluster tightly and yield stable ranking quality
while sampling 100 users at random demonstrates that the method generalizes across diverse profile sparsities
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; the per-user plot does not relate scores to profile sparsity.
assertions.reader_inference: The text relates no per-user score to any sparsity measure, so generalisation 'across diverse profile sparsities' is not shown by the reported material.

assertions.value: The authors list as future work deeper QAOA circuits or additional qubits, adaptive clustering or alternative dictionary-learning methods, and end-to-end tuning of clustering hyperparameters, RF feature limits and QAOA angles via Bayesian optimization.

Dynamic, user-driven cluster sizes or alternative dictionary-learning methods
Jointly optimizing clustering hyperparameters, RF feature limits, and QAOA angles via Bayesian optimization
